_note: 60 Seconds! / 60 Parsecs! style turn-based flight survival & engineering logbook (no countdown timer on questions). 24 conditional nodes: 4 gates x 3 missions x 2 states (critical / nominal).

critical.title: Rocket shaking hard at peak pressure!
critical.scenario_context: Your rocket is passing Max-Q, the moment of strongest air pressure. It is close to its weight limit and your reserve fund (UFE) is tight. What do you do?

options.label: Fund extra fuel margin (−5% reserve, +45 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spends emergency money now to gain fuel you can use later in the flight.

options.label: Drop extra brackets (−45 kg weight)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A lighter spacecraft stays safely under the rocket's limit. No money spent.

options.label: Fly as planned (no change)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Keeps your whole reserve for later problems, but leaves no safety margin now.

nominal.title: Liftoff went smoothly — what now?
nominal.scenario_context: Your rocket passed peak air pressure with weight and budget to spare. The upper stage is about to push you toward the Moon (Translunar Injection). What is your order?

options.label: Save leftover fuel (+30 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Extra fuel gives you room for course corrections later.

options.label: Warm up instruments early (+5 science, −3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Instruments that are ready sooner collect better data, but this uses some battery.

options.label: Put unused money in reserve (+3% reserve)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A bigger reserve fund helps you pay for emergencies later.

critical.title: Moon rocket shaking at peak pressure!
critical.scenario_context: Your Moon spacecraft is passing Max-Q, when air pressure on the rocket is strongest. Its fueled weight is near the rocket's limit and your reserve fund (UFE) is tight.

options.label: Fund extra fuel margin (−5% reserve, +45 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Uses emergency money now so you have more fuel later.

options.label: Drop spare adapter parts (−45 kg weight)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Lighter is safer for the rocket, and it costs nothing.

options.label: Fly as planned (no change)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves your reserve for problems near the Moon, but leaves no margin now.

nominal.title: Clean liftoff, heading to the Moon
nominal.scenario_context: Your rocket cleared the tower with weight and money to spare. Before the long coast to the Moon, how do you use the extra capacity?

options.label: Save leftover fuel (+30 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Extra fuel lets you fine-tune your path around the Moon.

options.label: Warm up the light sensor (+5 science, −3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A ready spectrometer, a tool that splits light, collects better Moon data.

options.label: Move ground savings to reserve (+3% reserve)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: More emergency money for the rest of the trip.

critical.title: Too heavy for the escape burn!
critical.scenario_context: You are firing the engine to escape Earth's gravity toward a near-Earth asteroid. The spacecraft's weight and cost are pushing the rocket adapter to its limit.

options.label: Drop the heavy separation ring early (−50 kg weight)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Less weight means each kilogram of fuel takes you farther.

options.label: Buy a small booster (−5% reserve, +55 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spends emergency money to give you more fuel for deep space.

options.label: Turn off a backup heater (+4% battery, −4 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves power, but instruments start out a little less ready.

nominal.title: Perfect escape from Earth
nominal.scenario_context: Your spacecraft left Earth's gravity right on course for the asteroid, with weight and reserve fund to spare. How do you use this good start?

options.label: Save braking fuel (+35 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: You will need fuel to slow down and fly close to the asteroid.

options.label: Calibrate the mineral sensor on stars (+5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A well-tuned infrared sensor identifies asteroid minerals more accurately.

options.label: Save unused launch money (+4% reserve)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: More emergency money for dodging boulders near the asteroid.

critical.title: Mars stack too heavy and over budget!
critical.scenario_context: Your Mars spacecraft, an orbiter plus a sample-return heat shield, is pushing the rocket's limits and the budget cap during the climb. What do you give up?

options.label: Drop cruise trim weights (−60 kg weight)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Cuts weight so the rocket is not overloaded.

options.label: Fund an upper-stage boost (−6% reserve, +65 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spends emergency money to make sure you have fuel to reach Mars.

options.label: Postpone extra ground work (−$35M cost, −5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves $35 million to stay under budget, but you lose some science.

nominal.title: Perfect push toward Mars
nominal.scenario_context: Over 52% of your spacecraft's weight is fuel, a good match for your heavy rocket. You are now cruising to Mars. What comes first?

options.label: Save fuel for Mars arrival (+45 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: You need a big braking burn to be captured into Mars orbit.

options.label: Align the cameras during cruise (+6 science, −3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Sharper cameras mean better Mars pictures, for a little battery.

options.label: Put launch savings in reserve (+4% reserve)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Extra emergency money before Mars dust storm season.

critical.title: Off-balance spacecraft is wasting fuel!
critical.scenario_context: During a course correction, the spacecraft's center of gravity is off-center (or fuel is tight). The thrusters fight the wobble and burn 1.5 times the normal fuel.

options.label: Re-balance with reaction wheels (normal fuel use, −7% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Electric spinning wheels steady the craft, so fuel use goes back to normal.

options.label: Re-balance by pumping fuel (−4% reserve, +50 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Fixes the balance and frees usable fuel, paid with ground support money.

options.label: Burn anyway without re-balancing (no change)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves battery and reserve, but you keep burning 1.5 times the fuel.

nominal.title: Balanced and right on course
nominal.scenario_context: Your center of gravity is well centered, so the main engine burns at normal efficiency. How do you shape your arrival orbit?

options.label: Fly lower to map (+6 science, −20 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A closer orbit gives sharper science data, using some spare fuel.

options.label: Take the low-energy route (+35 kg fuel, +3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves fuel and power for whatever space throws at you next.

options.label: Reset the steering wheels (+0.03 science quality)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A steadier spacecraft lets instruments take sharper readings.

critical.title: Wobbling near the Moon, wasting fuel!
critical.scenario_context: Approaching the Moon, an off-center center of gravity (or low fuel margin) makes the spacecraft wobble, and it burns 1.5 times the normal fuel. How do you steady it?

options.label: Re-balance with reaction wheels (normal fuel use, −7% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Gets fuel use back to normal, but drains battery.

options.label: Use Moon's gravity (balanced, −4% reserve, +55 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: The Moon's pull saves fuel; ground teams replan the route with reserve money.

options.label: Burn directly without re-balancing (no change)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves battery for solar storms, but you may run out of fuel.

nominal.title: Smooth, balanced flyby of the Moon
nominal.scenario_context: Your center of gravity stayed within the 0.25 m limit for the Moon mission, so the engine burn is clean and efficient. What do you do at closest approach?

options.label: Skim the polar crater (+6 science, −20 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spends a little fuel to study possible ice in polar craters.

options.label: Save fuel, charge batteries (+35 kg fuel, +4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Builds up survival reserves before crossing the radiation belts.

options.label: Aim the antenna at Earth (4.6 dB signal)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A steady craft can point its dish precisely for a stronger signal.

critical.title: Crooked braking burn near the asteroid!
critical.scenario_context: As you slow down to match the asteroid's path, unevenly placed instruments (or low fuel margin) make you burn 1.5 times the normal fuel. How do you fix it?

options.label: Tilt engine to re-balance (normal fuel use, −6% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Points the thrust through the true center of gravity using battery power.

options.label: Drop cover, re-balance (−40 kg weight, +40 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Fixes the balance, and the lighter craft gets more from its fuel.

options.label: Do a fast flyby instead of stopping (−8 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Less time to collect data, but saves battery and reserve.

nominal.title: Gentle braking next to the asteroid
nominal.scenario_context: Your center of gravity is balanced within 0.15 m, and you matched the asteroid's spin with fuel to spare. What is your next command?

options.label: Map from 1 km (+7 science, −20 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A very close orbit gives detailed mineral maps, using spare fuel.

options.label: Save fuel for a quick escape (+40 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Lets you back away fast if the surface sprays dust during sampling.

options.label: Charge the battery and onboard computers (+5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Gets power ready for the risky close approach.

critical.title: Mars arrival: balance problem!
critical.scenario_context: Approaching Mars, your spacecraft breaks its strict 0.08 m balance limit (or fuel is very short). It could skip off the Martian atmosphere instead of being captured.

options.label: Air-brake and re-balance (−7% battery, +60 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Thin upper air slows you down for free; wheels restore normal fuel use.

options.label: Shift fuel to re-balance (−5% reserve, +70 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Moves fuel from a backup tank to fix the balance; costs reserve money.

options.label: Drop a spare cruise shield (−55 kg weight)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A lighter craft makes the capture burn more likely to succeed.

nominal.title: Perfect capture into Mars orbit
nominal.scenario_context: Even with the strict 0.08 m Mars balance limit, your spacecraft stayed steady through the main engine burn. How do you adjust your orbit?

options.label: Enter low sun-synced orbit (+8 science, −25 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: The same lighting every pass gives the best close-up images of Jezero Crater.

options.label: Save fuel for the trip home (+50 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: The samples still need fuel to get back to Earth.

options.label: Warm and charge the batteries (+6% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: More battery power before Martian dust storms block the Sun.

critical.title: Space storm hits with low reserves!
critical.scenario_context: A strong space weather event hits while your battery, self-driving camera, or reserve fund is dangerously low. Check what you packed and choose.

options.label: Fund backup power, self-driving camera (−5% reserve, +12% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Emergency money restores the battery and turns on camera-based navigation.

options.label: Turn off heaters for power (+15% battery, −6 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Gives up a little science to keep power above safe-mode level.

options.label: Hide in safe mode (only 85% data delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Protects the spacecraft, but storm noise means less data reaches Earth.

nominal.title: Storm survived thanks to good packing
nominal.scenario_context: When the space hazard hit, your heat shield, power source, self-driving camera, and reserve fund absorbed it. How do you use this calm moment?

options.label: Measure the storm's light (+8 science, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Turns the hazard into bonus science using spare battery.

options.label: Boost the radio (4.5 dB signal, 100% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spare power makes sure the final data transfer to Earth goes smoothly.

options.label: Keep all reserves, top up battery (+5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Maximum safety margin all the way back to Earth.

critical.title: Solar storm hits on the way home!
critical.scenario_context: A burst of particles from the Sun sweeps between Earth and the Moon. Your battery is under 15% or your heat protection is weak, before re-entering Earth's air at 40,000 km/h.

options.label: Switch to backup power cells (−5% reserve, +12% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Keeps Orion's battery up so it does not drop into safe mode.

options.label: Put Moon cameras to sleep (+15% battery, −6 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Protects the systems needed for re-entry by pausing extra imaging.

options.label: Hide in safe mode (only 85% data delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Saves reserve money, but storm noise means less data reaches Earth.

nominal.title: Storm passed, heat shield ready
nominal.scenario_context: Your fuel cells and batteries (at least 15% charge) plus your heat shield handled the solar storm without losing contact. What is your order?

options.label: Study the solar flare's light (+8 science, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Rare readings of solar flare light earn bonus science.

options.label: Boost the radio (4.6 dB signal, 100% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Spare power guarantees a clean connection to Earth's big antennas.

options.label: Top up the re-entry battery (+5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Extra power for the 40,000 km/h plunge through Earth's air.

critical.title: Dust cloud blinds your navigation!
critical.scenario_context: Descending toward the asteroid, a cloud of gravel and dust blinds the cameras that steer by the stars. Without a self-driving camera or at least 15% reserve, crash risk is high.

options.label: Upload self-driving camera software (−8% reserve, −5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Lets the probe steer by recognizing surface features, paid with ground support money.

options.label: Retreat, enable self-driving camera (−5% reserve, −25 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Burns fuel to clear the dust, then locks on with camera navigation.

options.label: Stay high above the surface (−8 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Avoids the boulders, but you collect fewer close-up readings.

nominal.title: Safe touch-and-go between boulders
nominal.scenario_context: Your self-driving camera, which steers by recognizing surface features, and a reserve fund of 15% or more guided the probe past the giant boulder nicknamed Mount Doom. What next?

options.label: Scan extra surface dust (+9 science, −3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Close-range infrared readings reveal water-bearing minerals.

options.label: Boost the radio (4.5 dB signal, 100% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Makes sure all 160 gigabits of asteroid data reach Earth.

options.label: Puff gas to clean solar panels (+5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Dust-free panels make more power after leaving the dust cloud.

critical.title: Dust storm and a stuck sample arm!
critical.scenario_context: A Martian dust storm cuts sunlight to 43% and the sample arm jams. Without a nuclear battery (RTG) or 25% battery, plus a 20% reserve, half the sample tubes are at risk.

options.label: Shake the arm free (−8% reserve, +12% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Vibration frees the stuck arm and backup power refills the battery.

options.label: Reroute heater power (+15% battery, −6% reserve, −6 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Moves power to the arm so every sample tube is loaded in time.

options.label: Launch now with the tubes you have (no change)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Guarantees the small rocket leaves Mars, but some tubes stay behind.

nominal.title: Nuclear power beats the dust storm
nominal.scenario_context: Dust darkened the Martian sky, but your nuclear battery (RTG) or high charge, plus a 20% reserve, kept the arm warm. Every sample tube is sealed in its capsule.

options.label: Run an extra life-sign scan (+9 science, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Uses spare power to double-check the tubes for signs of past life.

options.label: Power the relay dish (4.6 dB signal, 100% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Keeps the Mars-to-Earth link well above the 3 dB minimum.

options.label: Save power for the trip home (+6% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Maximum safety margin for the return orbiter that catches the samples.

critical.title: Weak signal, memory full of data!
critical.scenario_context: Solar noise and huge distance have dropped your signal margin below the 3 dB minimum for NASA's Deep Space Network antennas, while 160 gigabits of science wait in memory.

options.label: Compress data (3.4 dB signal, 96% delivered, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Sends the most valuable science first and re-locks the signal, using some battery.

options.label: Boost antenna (3.8 dB signal, 100% delivered, −5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Turns off some instruments to push their power into the antenna.

options.label: Send slowly and safely (3.2 dB signal, 78% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A slow, steady signal is reliable, but not all the data gets home.

nominal.title: Big antenna locked on Earth
nominal.scenario_context: Your signal is well above the 3 dB minimum and the control channel is clear. How do you send the final 160 gigabits of science to Earth?

options.label: Send the full archive (100% delivered, +5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Everything reaches Earth, including bonus calibrated readings.

options.label: Compare with lab standards (100% delivered, +0.04 science quality)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Comparing with reference samples on Earth makes your results more accurate.

options.label: Send at normal speed (100% delivered, +3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: All the data arrives while you save battery.

critical.title: Moon about to block your signal!
critical.scenario_context: Soon the Moon will block your line of sight to Earth. Your radio signal margin is below 3 dB and the 160-gigabit recorder is still full. Pick a plan.

options.label: Compress data (3.4 dB signal, 96% delivered, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Sends the key ice and light data first, before contact is lost.

options.label: Boost antenna (3.8 dB signal, 100% delivered, −5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Moves spare power to the dish; some extra science is lost.

options.label: Send slowly and safely (3.2 dB signal, 78% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Sturdier error-proof coding keeps the link, but only part gets through.

nominal.title: Clear signal, getting ready to splash down
nominal.scenario_context: Your signal is locked above 3 dB on the Deep Space Network station in Madrid, and the heat shield is ready. The 160-gigabit recorder is sending smoothly. Final order?

options.label: Send all Moon data (100% delivered, +5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Every bit of Moon science gets home.

options.label: Compare with lab standards (100% delivered, +0.04 science quality)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Improves the accuracy of your light readings before splashdown.

options.label: Normal send, save re-entry power (100% delivered, +3% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: All the data arrives and you keep extra battery for splashdown.

critical.title: So far away the signal fades!
critical.scenario_context: Millions of kilometers from Earth, the radio signal spreads out and weakens, dropping your margin below 3 dB. 160 gigabits of asteroid mineral maps wait in memory.

options.label: Compress data (3.5 dB signal, 96% delivered, −4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Packs the mineral readings tightly without losing detail, using some battery.

options.label: Boost antenna (3.9 dB signal, 100% delivered, −5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Turns off the wide-view camera so its power goes to the radio.

options.label: Send key minerals slowly (3.2 dB signal, 78% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Steady and safe, but part of the dataset stays on board.

nominal.title: Strong 4.2 dB link to Earth
nominal.scenario_context: Your signal code unlocked the radio, and your 3 m dish holds a solid link above 3 dB to the giant 70 m Goldstone antenna in California. How do you finish?

options.label: Send full 3D asteroid map (100% delivered, +6 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: All the data arrives, with bonus science from the boulder and mineral map.

options.label: Compare with lab standards (100% delivered, +0.04 science quality)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Matching mineral readings to a reference library makes results more accurate.

options.label: Normal send, save fuel (100% delivered, +25 kg fuel)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Leftover fuel could let the mission visit more places later.

critical.title: The Sun is about to block Mars!
critical.scenario_context: Soon Mars passes behind the Sun, cutting contact for about two weeks. Signals already take 4 to 25 minutes each way, and your margin is under 3 dB. Act now!

options.label: Rush data (3.5 dB signal, 96% delivered, −5% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Gets the sample list and life-sign readings home before the blackout.

options.label: Boost antenna (3.9 dB signal, 100% delivered, −5 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Turns off the radar so its power goes to the dish.

options.label: Store the rest (3.2 dB signal, 78% delivered)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Keeps a safe link now; the rest waits in memory until after the blackout.

nominal.title: Fast link to Earth before the blackout
nominal.scenario_context: Your 3 m antenna is locked above 3 dB onto Deep Space Network stations in Australia and California, emptying the 160-gigabit recorder before the Sun blocks Mars.

options.label: Send all Mars data (100% delivered, +7 science)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: Every gigabit reaches Earth with the most science possible.

options.label: Compare with lab standards (100% delivered, +0.04 science quality)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: A lab reference sharpens the life-sign readings.

options.label: Finish sending, save capsule power (100% delivered, +4% battery)
options.engineering_tradeoff_hint: All the data arrives and the return capsule keeps extra power.

random_events._note: Random survival events (2026-11-15). One per match, seeded by room PIN + mission in decision_tree.pick_random_event. Effect sizes are game estimates (estado: estimado del juego); the phenomena are real (fuente).

artemis_moon.title: Solar radiation storm
artemis_moon.description: A solar flare floods the cabin path with protons. Heaters and shielding drain the batteries.
artemis_moon.mitigation_text: The RTG kept power steady through the storm.

artemis_moon.title: Micrometeoroid strike
artemis_moon.description: A sand-grain-sized particle punches the hull. Repairs eat into the reserve fund.
artemis_moon.mitigation_text: The heat shield layers absorbed most of the hit.

artemis_moon.title: Ground station dropout
artemis_moon.description: A Deep Space Network antenna goes offline for maintenance. The link gets weaker.
artemis_moon.mitigation_text: Your clean signal code let a backup antenna lock on fast.

asteroid_hunter.title: Asteroid particle ejection
asteroid_hunter.description: The asteroid sheds pebbles like Bennu did. Navigating around them costs reserve.
asteroid_hunter.mitigation_text: Self-driving navigation dodged the debris on its own.

asteroid_hunter.title: Solar radiation storm
asteroid_hunter.description: A solar flare hits deep space. Shielding drains the batteries.
asteroid_hunter.mitigation_text: The RTG kept power steady through the storm.

asteroid_hunter.title: Ground station dropout
asteroid_hunter.description: A Deep Space Network antenna goes offline. The link gets weaker.
asteroid_hunter.mitigation_text: Your clean signal code let a backup antenna lock on fast.

mars_sample_return.title: Global dust storm
mars_sample_return.description: A planet-wide dust storm blocks the Sun for weeks. Solar power collapses.
mars_sample_return.mitigation_text: Nuclear power does not need sunlight: the RTG carried you through.

mars_sample_return.title: Solar conjunction
mars_sample_return.description: Mars slips behind the Sun. Radio signals pass through solar plasma and get noisy.
mars_sample_return.mitigation_text: Your error-checked signal code survived the noise.

mars_sample_return.title: Micrometeoroid strike
mars_sample_return.description: A tiny particle punches the hull. Repairs eat into the reserve fund.
mars_sample_return.mitigation_text: The heat shield layers absorbed most of the hit.

_difficulty._note: Difficulty tuning (2026-11-15, estimado del juego): harder missions face more and harsher hazards. count = events per match, scale = effect multiplier when not mitigated.
